title: How to organize Claude Code for product work
excerpt: Download the starter workspace. Run the setup skill. Sort files by how fast they change. Turn repeated work into skills. File every correction once.
content_html:
My Claude Code workspace for my product job is a folder with almost no code in it. It holds a context folder with everything about the company: the product, the users, the competitors, how I like to work. One folder per project, with the tasks separated from the deliverables. A set of skills that each do one recurring piece of work: the status update, the PRD review, the interview synthesis. When I give feedback once, it lands in a file with a note on why, and I never give that feedback again. I didn’t design this system. I arrived at it, mostly by getting it wrong first.

Getting it wrong taught me the lesson that runs this whole article. Past the basics, your results in Claude Code stop depending on how well you prompt and start depending on how well you file. A good prompt improves one session; a good file improves every session after it. The prompt-tuning advice you’ve already read stops helping at exactly the point where the filing starts to matter.

So instead of describing my system, I packaged it. The starter workspace is public on GitHub: the folders, the context templates, and five PM skills, personalized by one setup interview. You don’t need to be technical to follow along; every step is spelled out, including installing the tools. And while my example is a product job, the same architecture fits any context-heavy work: a design lead’s research library, a data team’s metric definitions, a founder’s everything-folder.

Here’s the route.

  • The switch. I’ll show you what chat mode and Cowork can’t give you, and why the terminal is worth it for a product manager.

  • The starter workspace. Download it, run one setup skill, and give it a real task: six steps, each shown on screen.

  • The practices. Six moves that make the system compound, each one naming the exact thing to do and what you get back.

  • The rhythm. Here’s what a normal workday looks like inside the system, from the first short prompt to the two-minute filing habit.

The payoff is concrete. One sitting gets you running: install the tools, download the workspace, answer the setup interview, hand over a first real task. You stop re-explaining your company every session, and every correction you make becomes permanent. Every step is below.

Time to open the filing cabinet.

You probably run your product work through Claude’s chat today: a browser tab or the desktop app, maybe Cowork for the agentic tasks. It works, and that’s exactly the trap. Every conversation starts from zero. The strategy doc you uploaded last time is gone, the context you patiently explained lives in a thread you’ll never find again, and the output you liked is trapped inside a conversation instead of sitting in a file. Chat is a great place to think and a terrible place to accumulate. For occasional questions that’s fine. For daily product work, it means paying the same setup cost every single morning.

Claude Code is the same Claude with a different home: a folder on your machine that it can read, navigate, and write to. Context lives in files that persist. Recurring work lives in skills that run on command. Outputs land as documents you keep, not messages you scroll for. In my daily use, everything I used to do in chat or Cowork runs better here, because nothing is ever explained twice. That’s an observation from my own work, not a law, but it’s held for months.

The part that actually changed my job is the terminal underneath. Claude Code speaks to GitHub natively, no connector needed: it can pull a company repository and answer questions about it, and it can push your own work. Ask it to fetch the repo behind your product and explain what a feature flag actually does. Push your workspace to a private repository and a teammate can clone it and inherit your head start. For a product manager, that’s a direct line into the codebase and a way to share your whole system, both of which chat simply doesn’t have.

What nobody hands you is the filing system that makes all this compound. Anthropic’s best-practices guide is written, in its own words, “for engineers using Claude Code across various codebases, languages, and environments,” and engineers get their structure free: the codebase is already organized context. The PM guides that exist, Sachin Rekhi’s being the best known, rightly tell you to “store all of your product data and documentation in local markdown files,” then move on. Organized how? Try it without an answer and you get what I had: forty loose files and a stale setup. The starter workspace is that answer, prebuilt. Let’s set it up.

The starter workspace is the structure I run my own product work on, cleaned into a template: the folders, the context files with guided placeholders, an example project, and five skills already installed. The whole thing is free and public: claude-code-pm-starter. Six steps take you from nothing to a first real task, and none of them assume a technical background.

One prerequisites note before you start. You need a paid Claude plan for Claude Code. Everything else, including the two tools you’ll install, is free and covered in the steps.

Claude Code runs in a terminal, and a terminal alone is a bad home for a product manager: you can’t see your files. The fix is an IDE. An IDE is just an editor that shows your folder as a panel of files while you work; developers live in one all day, and you’ll borrow it for the file panel alone. Download VS Code, the free standard, and install it like any app. You won’t write code in it. You’ll watch your workspace organize itself in the left panel, which is exactly the visibility chat mode never gave you.

Open the repository page, click the green Code button, and choose Download ZIP. No git, no account needed. Unzip it and move the folder wherever you keep your work. This folder is about to become the place your product work lives, so pick somewhere you’ll find it again, like a work folder in your home directory.

Open VS Code, choose File > Open Folder, and pick the unzipped folder. The left panel now shows the whole structure: context/, projects/, operations/, the skills. Then open the terminal inside VS Code with Terminal > New Terminal, and here’s the small trick that changes how the whole thing feels: right-click the terminal panel’s header and choose Move Panel Right. Files on the left, agent on the right: it stops feeling like a command line and starts feeling like a colleague sitting next to your documents.

If you don’t have Claude Code yet, install it now from the official guide; it’s one command pasted into that terminal. Then type claude and press Enter. Claude Code starts inside the folder, reads the map file, and knows where everything lives from your first message.

One distinction saves beginners a lot of confusion. The terminal wants exact commands; Claude wants normal language. Before you typed claude, you were talking to the terminal, where spelling and syntax matter. Now that Claude Code is running, you’re talking to Claude, exactly like in the chat app. So do the natural first thing: type hello and ask it what it can see in this folder. It will answer like a colleague who just read your files.

A few slash commands are worth knowing on day one, typed directly into Claude Code:

  • /model - shows which Claude model you’re running and lets you switch.

  • /effort - sets how much thinking Claude puts into each answer; higher effort for hard work, lower for quick drafts.

  • /mcp - lists your MCPs, the live connections into tools like Jira, Slack, or Confluence, and lets you manage them.

  • /plugins - opens the plugin system, and this one deserves a minute. Claude Code comes with Anthropic’s plugin directory available by default, and marketplaces can be added on top. One is built specifically for product managers: pm-skills, a hundred-plus PM skills across discovery, strategy, execution, and launch; its README has the up-to-date install instructions. pm-execution covers PRDs, OKRs, roadmaps, and retrospectives; pm-product-discovery adds interviews and assumption testing. Install the two or three that match your work, not all nine; every installed plugin is context the system carries.

One more control, then you’re done with the tour: press Shift+Tab to cycle Claude Code’s three modes.

  • Default mode asks your permission before touching any file.

  • Auto-accept applies edits without asking.

  • Plan mode is the one to remember: Claude researches and proposes a plan, and nothing changes until you approve it.

Start in default, use plan mode for anything big, and save auto-accept for work you’ve learned to trust. For everything beyond these, this community cheat sheet is the best one-page reference I’ve found.

Type /setup-workspace and press Enter. The workspace ships with a skill whose only job is to personalize the template: it interviews you about your company, your product, your users, and how you like to work, then fills in the context files and renames the example project to your most active real one. Answer in plain language; it does the writing and shows you each file for a yes or a fix.

You don’t have to answer from memory: paste links. Hand it your product’s public site, a documentation page, or, if you connected the Atlassian MCP in the previous step, the Confluence page about your team, and it reads them and builds the context files from what’s already written. Fifteen minutes of this replaces the blank-page problem entirely. Your exact questions will differ a little from mine; each session is a little unpredictable, that’s just how these models work. Skip anything you don’t know yet; an honest placeholder beats invented content.

Don’t end the first session on setup; hand it something you actually owe someone. Type /status-update and watch it draft your update from the project’s task file instead of your memory. Or point it at a real deliverable:

Draft the kickoff brief for [your project]. Match my writing preferences in context/preferences.md. Check the open questions in the project’s tasks.md before concluding anything.

The first output that sounds like you, about your product, with your project’s real state in it, is the moment the filing clicks. Three more skills wait in the folder: prd-review for the next document you’d like a hard read on, interview-synthesis for your next user conversation, and file-feedback, the one that makes your corrections permanent.

That’s the start: a working system in one sitting. What makes it compound is how you feed it, and that’s six practices.

The starter structure encodes the practices I converged on by getting each one wrong first. They’re not a methodology to obey; they’re the moves that kept earning their place. Each one below names the concrete thing to do and what you get back for it. The first one is the engine; the rest steer.

The single highest-return habit is also the simplest to state: default to the workspace for everything. Each time a task lands on you, open the workspace and do it there with Claude Code, even when chat would feel faster. The first run of a new kind of task takes longer, I won’t pretend otherwise: you explain, you correct, you adjust. But every explanation lands in a file, so the second run starts ahead, and the third barely needs you. It’s like teaching an intern: the first delegation costs you an afternoon, and then the work comes back done. A task kept in chat mode teaches the system nothing; the same task done in the workspace is an investment that pays on every repeat.

The habit has a closing move, and it’s where the compounding actually happens. When a task is done and you’re satisfied with the result, don’t just close the terminal. Ask Claude to bank what it learned: convert the finished task into a skill if it will repeat, confirm the new facts into the context files, and update your preferences file with the feedback you gave along the way. I say it almost in those words: “we’re done, turn this into a skill, and file the corrections I made.” That one sentence at the end of a task is the difference between a tool you use and a system that learns.

The organizing question surprised me. It isn’t “what topic does this belong to?” It’s “how fast does this change?” Everything in your work has a speed: your product’s positioning barely moves, a status summary lasts about a week, a ticket queue changes by the hour. File things by their speed, and stale can never masquerade as fresh. File them by topic, and old truth sits next to current truth, looking identical.

The three folders in the workspace are the three speeds. The concrete habit: the next meeting note you take goes into operations/ with the date in the filename, and the paragraph you keep retyping about your product goes into context/product.md. A note was true the day you wrote it, so the date travels in the filename where Claude reads it; the positioning paragraph is true until you change it, so it lives where every session can load it. Projects sit between the two speeds, which is why each project folder splits tasks.md from brief.md.

There’s a third speed, and you already own it.

MCPs, those live connections from Step 4, sit at the fast end of the spectrum: they’re for what changes hourly. Files are for what changes slowly. If you’re pasting live data into a context file, an MCP should own it; if you’re re-fetching stable truth through an MCP every session, a file should own it. If you’ve used PARA, Tiago Forte’s filing method, this rhymes with it, with one difference: PARA sorts by actionability, because a human’s failure mode is losing track of what to act on. This system sorts by rate of change, because an LLM’s failure mode is stale context confidently reused.

CLAUDE.md is the one file every session loads: the map that says who you are, what lives where, and the few rules that always apply. Here’s the honest practice: you almost never touch it by hand. If you’re organizing an existing folder rather than using the starter workspace, the /init command creates it for you: Claude scans the folder and writes the map itself. From then on, maintenance happens as a side effect: when you add a skill or a context file, Claude updates the map to match, and your job is just to say yes.

The one thing worth knowing is why the map stays small. It loads into every session, relevant or not, so every line spends a little of what Anthropic’s context-engineering post calls the “attention budget”; their docs target under 200 lines and warn that bloated files make Claude ignore your actual instructions. The map points, the files carry: knowledge lives in context/, loaded only when a task needs it. I wrote about this just-in-time principle in How to build an AI helper for your team with Cowork; here, Claude applies it for you.

I carried a doubt about this practice for months. My habit is to look at every recurring piece of work and ask whether it can become a skill, so I give the feedback once and never redo the work again. It felt productive, and I wasn’t sure it was right, because nothing written for product people says where skills end and files begin. The test that settled it: nouns go in files, verbs go in skills. What Claude needs to know is a noun: product facts, user segments, terminology, in context/. What Claude needs to do is a verb: draft, review, synthesize, each one a skill.

In practice, skills come from the closing move of the first practice: you finish a task, you’re satisfied, and you ask Claude to turn what you just did together into a skill. The workspace’s status-update skill shows what one looks like: where it reads from, what shape the output takes, what quality bar it checks. Steps, a quality bar, an output format: that’s what a skill encodes, and that’s why “the roadmap review prep” or “the churn digest” qualify while “that one weird escalation” doesn’t. If you want to build one from scratch instead, How to build your first Claude Code skill walks through it step by step.

The test also catches the two ways things end up in the wrong drawer.

The first mismatch is a “skill” that’s really a fact bucket: product context wearing a skill’s clothes, never doing anything. That becomes a context file. The second is the reverse: a procedure written as notes inside context/, like a “how I run reviews” paragraph nobody can execute. A documented-but-not-executable procedure gets re-explained anyway, which defeats the whole point. That one becomes a skill. The know/do split is how documentation practice has organized itself for a decade (Diátaxis formalizes it); skills just make the “do” side executable.

You know the moment. Claude drafts your status update, and you fix the same phrasing you’ve already fixed once. Here’s the reframe that changed my week-to-week: a correction made in chat is perishable; it’s gone when the session ends. The entire compounding return of the system comes from making corrections permanent, and this is where the practices stop being organization and start being learning.

The simplest version is the one to start with, and it’s the highest-return edit in this article. Open context/preferences.md and write three lines about how you write: sentence length, what your documents open with, the words you ban. From then on, every document Claude drafts comes out aligned with your writing preferences instead of sounding like a press release. That’s one correction, filed once, applied to everything that follows. The oldest entries in my own preferences file are corrections I have never had to give again.

For everything past that first edit, the workspace ships a skill that does the filing for you. When you catch yourself correcting something, run /file-feedback. It routes the correction with four questions.

Was it a one-off slip? Let it go; not everything deserves a file. A missing fact? It goes to the matching context file or the project’s brief. A wrong process? The fix goes into the skill, so it runs correctly every time after. Taste? It becomes a preferences entry, and here’s the detail that matters: each entry gets a line on why and a line on how to apply it, so future sessions can judge edge cases instead of pattern-matching blindly.

It turns out the vendor agrees, in almost the same words. Anthropic’s memory docs tell you to write things down when “Claude makes the same mistake a second time” or when “you type the same correction or clarification into chat that you typed last session.” The best-practices guide promises the payoff in one line: “The file compounds in value over time.” So here’s the version I’d put on a sticky note, and the line I’d hand your team: if you’ve said it twice, it belongs in a file.

The last practice removes a blocker that sits in your head, not in your files. You’ll catch yourself assuming a thing is out of reach: too technical, too long, needs a tutorial, needs an engineer. The move is to ask Claude Code first and let the answer surprise you. I wanted to try AWS Amplify, Amazon’s service for building and hosting apps, and my reflex was the old one: follow the guidelines, read the documentation, budget hours I didn’t have. Instead I pasted the documentation link into Claude Code and asked for two things: a working prototype to test the service, and a step-by-step guide written for someone non-technical. In one sitting I had something I could actually release, plus a guide I could follow and understand. The hours I had budgeted were never spent.

The same reflex applies at every scale, not just new tools. Before you summarize the forty-page research report yourself, ask. Before you assume the data question needs an analyst, ask. Before you check every intermediate step, give the whole task with the constraints and verify the result instead. The system you’ve built through the first five practices is exactly what makes asking cheap: the context is filed, the preferences are known, and a wrong answer costs you a correction, which the system then keeps. Six practices, one architecture. Here’s what it feels like on a normal workday.

A day inside the system looks less like chatting and more like working with a very fast colleague who reads the files first.

Sessions start in the project folder, not a blank chat. I open the workspace in VS Code, launch claude in the terminal, and the map loads with every file path ready to use. The task file already says where things stand, what’s blocked, and what’s next, because the previous session updated it. My first prompt names the goal and points at files by name, and it stays short on purpose. Prompting shrinks as filing grows. A good prompt in this system has three parts: the goal in one sentence, the non-negotiable constraints, and what to verify before showing you. About a hundred words, often less. The steps live in skills, the background lives in files, and the prompt only has to steer. For bigger work I add one move: switch to plan mode with Shift+Tab and approve the plan before anything runs.

The habit that holds it all together takes two minutes at the end of a session, and the file-feedback skill carries most of it. Three questions: did I correct anything I’ve corrected before, did a new fact surface that isn’t filed anywhere, did a piece of work repeat again? Repeat corrections go through the router; repeated work gets nominated as the next skill. Skip the ceremony when the answer is three nos, which is most sessions.

Every dozen sessions or so, I spend fifteen minutes pruning, and I’d argue this is the least optional part. Stale context is worse than missing context. An expired competitor note or an outdated positioning line doesn’t look stale to Claude; it gets woven into new work with full confidence, and Anthropic’s best-practices guide carries a matching warning: when two rules contradict each other, Claude may pick one arbitrarily. So: date-stamp what’s dated, archive closed projects, delete anything you wouldn’t want quoted back to you in a draft. That’s the whole system, running. What’s left is to start it.

What changed for me isn’t that Claude got smarter. It’s that I stopped having the same conversation twice. The company explanation I used to retype lives in context/. The feedback I used to repeat lives in skills and a preferences file. The projects pick up where they left off. The system’s real product is quiet: shorter prompts, fewer corrections, sessions that start in the middle of the work instead of at the beginning of my job description.

The shape travels well beyond product management. A discovery-heavy PM files interview syntheses as dated outputs and lets a skill do the synthesizing. A platform PM’s stable context is API consumers and versioning policy. A founder turns the investor update into a skill fed by a metrics file. A design lead files critique standards once instead of re-explaining them in every review. A data lead’s metric definitions become the context file every teammate’s sessions read. Different jobs, same three drawers, same habit.

Start smaller than feels ambitious. Download the starter workspace, run the setup interview, and add those three lines about how you write. Then bring it your very next task, and the one after that. The next time you catch yourself telling Claude Code something for the second time, you’ll know exactly where it goes. And soon enough, you won’t remember the last time you said it.

Each time a task lands on you, open the workspace and do it there with Claude Code, even when chat would feel faster. The first run of a new kind of task takes longer, I won’t pretend otherwise: you explain, you correct, you adjust. But every explanation lands in a file, so the second run starts ahead, and the third barely needs you. It’s like teaching an intern: the first delegation costs you an afternoon, and then the work comes back done. A task kept in chat mode teaches the system nothing; the same task done in the workspace is an investment that pays on every repeat.The habit has a closing move, and it’s where the compounding actually happens. When a task is done and you’re satisfied with the result, don’t just close the terminal. Ask Claude to bank what it learned: convert the finished task into a skill if it will repeat, confirm the new facts into the context files, and update your preferences file with the feedback you gave along the way. I say it almost in those words: “we’re done, turn this into a skill, and file the corrections I made.” That one sentence at the end of a task is the difference between a tool you use and a system that learns.The organizing question surprised me. It isn’t “what topic does this belong to?” It’s “how fast does this change?” Everything in your work has a speed: your product’s positioning barely moves, a status summary lasts about a week, a ticket queue changes by the hour. File things by their speed, and stale can never masquerade as fresh. File them by topic, and old truth sits next to current truth, looking identical.The three folders in the workspace are the three speeds. The concrete habit: the next meeting note you take goes into operations/ with the date in the filename, and the paragraph you keep retyping about your product goes into context/product.md. A note was true the day you wrote it, so the date travels in the filename where Claude reads it; the positioning paragraph is true until you change it, so it lives where every session can load it. Projects sit between the two speeds, which is why each project folder splits tasks.md from brief.md.There’s a third speed, and you already own it.MCPs, those live connections from Step 4, sit at the fast end of the spectrum: they’re for what changes hourly. Files are for what changes slowly. If you’re pasting live data into a context file, an MCP should own it; if you’re re-fetching stable truth through an MCP every session, a file should own it. If you’ve used PARA, Tiago Forte’s filing method, this rhymes with it, with one difference: PARA sorts by actionability, because a human’s failure mode is losing track of what to act on. This system sorts by rate of change, because an LLM’s failure mode is stale context confidently reused.CLAUDE.md is the one file every session loads: the map that says who you are, what lives where, and the few rules that always apply. Here’s the honest practice: you almost never touch it by hand. If you’re organizing an existing folder rather than using the starter workspace, the /init command creates it for you: Claude scans the folder and writes the map itself. From then on, maintenance happens as a side effect: when you add a skill or a context file, Claude updates the map to match, and your job is just to say yes.The one thing worth knowing is why the map stays small. It loads into every session, relevant or not, so every line spends a little of what Anthropic’s context-engineering post calls the “attention budget”; their docs target under 200 lines and warn that bloated files make Claude ignore your actual instructions. The map points, the files carry: knowledge lives in context/, loaded only when a task needs it. I wrote about this just-in-time principle in How to build an AI helper for your team with Cowork; here, Claude applies it for you.I carried a doubt about this practice for months. My habit is to look at every recurring piece of work and ask whether it can become a skill, so I give the feedback once and never redo the work again. It felt productive, and I wasn’t sure it was right, because nothing written for product people says where skills end and files begin. The test that settled it: nouns go in files, verbs go in skills. What Claude needs to know is a noun: product facts, user segments, terminology, in context/. What Claude needs to do is a verb: draft, review, synthesize, each one a skill.In practice, skills come from the closing move of the first practice: you finish a task, you’re satisfied, and you ask Claude to turn what you just did together into a skill. The workspace’s status-update skill shows what one looks like: where it reads from, what shape the output takes, what quality bar it checks. Steps, a quality bar, an output format: that’s what a skill encodes, and that’s why “the roadmap review prep” or “the churn digest” qualify while “that one weird escalation” doesn’t. If you want to build one from scratch instead, How to build your first Claude Code skill walks through it step by step.The test also catches the two ways things end up in the wrong drawer.The first mismatch is a “skill” that’s really a fact bucket: product context wearing a skill’s clothes, never doing anything. That becomes a context file. The second is the reverse: a procedure written as notes inside context/, like a “how I run reviews” paragraph nobody can execute. A documented-but-not-executable procedure gets re-explained anyway, which defeats the whole point. That one becomes a skill. The know/do split is how documentation practice has organized itself for a decade (Diátaxis formalizes it); skills just make the “do” side executable.You know the moment. Claude drafts your status update, and you fix the same phrasing you’ve already fixed once. Here’s the reframe that changed my week-to-week: a correction made in chat is perishable; it’s gone when the session ends. The entire compounding return of the system comes from making corrections permanent, and this is where the practices stop being organization and start being learning.The simplest version is the one to start with, and it’s the highest-return edit in this article. Open context/preferences.md and write three lines about how you write: sentence length, what your documents open with, the words you ban. From then on, every document Claude drafts comes out aligned with your writing preferences instead of sounding like a press release. That’s one correction, filed once, applied to everything that follows. The oldest entries in my own preferences file are corrections I have never had to give again.For everything past that first edit, the workspace ships a skill that does the filing for you. When you catch yourself correcting something, run /file-feedback. It routes the correction with four questions.Was it a one-off slip? Let it go; not everything deserves a file. A missing fact? It goes to the matching context file or the project’s brief. A wrong process? The fix goes into the skill, so it runs correctly every time after. Taste? It becomes a preferences entry, and here’s the detail that matters: each entry gets a line on why and a line on how to apply it, so future sessions can judge edge cases instead of pattern-matching blindly.It turns out the vendor agrees, in almost the same words. Anthropic’s memory docs tell you to write things down when “Claude makes the same mistake a second time” or when “you type the same correction or clarification into chat that you typed last session.” The best-practices guide promises the payoff in one line: “The file compounds in value over time.” So here’s the version I’d put on a sticky note, and the line I’d hand your team: if you’ve said it twice, it belongs in a file.The last practice removes a blocker that sits in your head, not in your files. You’ll catch yourself assuming a thing is out of reach: too technical, too long, needs a tutorial, needs an engineer. The move is to ask Claude Code first and let the answer surprise you. I wanted to try AWS Amplify, Amazon’s service for building and hosting apps, and my reflex was the old one: follow the guidelines, read the documentation, budget hours I didn’t have. Instead I pasted the documentation link into Claude Code and asked for two things: a working prototype to test the service, and a step-by-step guide written for someone non-technical. In one sitting I had something I could actually release, plus a guide I could follow and understand. The hours I had budgeted were never spent.The same reflex applies at every scale, not just new tools. Before you summarize the forty-page research report yourself, ask. Before you assume the data question needs an analyst, ask. Before you check every intermediate step, give the whole task with the constraints and verify the result instead. The system you’ve built through the first five practices is exactly what makes asking cheap: the context is filed, the preferences are known, and a wrong answer costs you a correction, which the system then keeps. Six practices, one architecture. Here’s what it feels like on a normal workday.A day inside the system looks less like chatting and more like working with a very fast colleague who reads the files first.Sessions start in the project folder, not a blank chat. I open the workspace in VS Code, launch claude in the terminal, and the map loads with every file path ready to use. The task file already says where things stand, what’s blocked, and what’s next, because the previous session updated it. My first prompt names the goal and points at files by name, and it stays short on purpose. Prompting shrinks as filing grows. A good prompt in this system has three parts: the goal in one sentence, the non-negotiable constraints, and what to verify before showing you. About a hundred words, often less. The steps live in skills, the background lives in files, and the prompt only has to steer. For bigger work I add one move: switch to plan mode with Shift+Tab and approve the plan before anything runs.The habit that holds it all together takes two minutes at the end of a session, and the file-feedback skill carries most of it. Three questions: did I correct anything I’ve corrected before, did a new fact surface that isn’t filed anywhere, did a piece of work repeat again? Repeat corrections go through the router; repeated work gets nominated as the next skill. Skip the ceremony when the answer is three nos, which is most sessions.Every dozen sessions or so, I spend fifteen minutes pruning, and I’d argue this is the least optional part. Stale context is worse than missing context. An expired competitor note or an outdated positioning line doesn’t look stale to Claude; it gets woven into new work with full confidence, and Anthropic’s best-practices guide carries a matching warning: when two rules contradict each other, Claude may pick one arbitrarily. So: date-stamp what’s dated, archive closed projects, delete anything you wouldn’t want quoted back to you in a draft. That’s the whole system, running. What’s left is to start it.What changed for me isn’t that Claude got smarter. It’s that I stopped having the same conversation twice. The company explanation I used to retype lives in context/. The feedback I used to repeat lives in skills and a preferences file. The projects pick up where they left off. The system’s real product is quiet: shorter prompts, fewer corrections, sessions that start in the middle of the work instead of at the beginning of my job description.The shape travels well beyond product management. A discovery-heavy PM files interview syntheses as dated outputs and lets a skill do the synthesizing. A platform PM’s stable context is API consumers and versioning policy. A founder turns the investor update into a skill fed by a metrics file. A design lead files critique standards once instead of re-explaining them in every review. A data lead’s metric definitions become the context file every teammate’s sessions read. Different jobs, same three drawers, same habit.Start smaller than feels ambitious. Download the starter workspace, run the setup interview, and add those three lines about how you write. Then bring it your very next task, and the one after that. The next time you catch yourself telling Claude Code something for the second time, you’ll know exactly where it goes. And soon enough, you won’t remember the last time you said it.No posts

blocks.html_en: Claude Code runs in a terminal, and a terminal alone is a bad home for a product manager: you can’t see your files. The fix is an IDE. An IDE is just an editor that shows your folder as a panel of files while you work; developers live in one all day, and you’ll borrow it for the file panel alone. Download VS Code, the free standard, and install it like any app. You won’t write code in it. You’ll watch your workspace organize itself in the left panel, which is exactly the visibility chat mode never gave you.

blocks.html_en: The single highest-return habit is also the simplest to state: default to the workspace for everything. Each time a task lands on you, open the workspace and do it there with Claude Code, even when chat would feel faster. The first run of a new kind of task takes longer, I won’t pretend otherwise: you explain, you correct, you adjust. But every explanation lands in a file, so the second run starts ahead, and the third barely needs you. It’s like teaching an intern: the first delegation costs you an afternoon, and then the work comes back done. A task kept in chat mode teaches the system nothing; the same task done in the workspace is an investment that pays on every repeat.

blocks.html_en: The habit has a closing move, and it’s where the compounding actually happens. When a task is done and you’re satisfied with the result, don’t just close the terminal. Ask Claude to bank what it learned: convert the finished task into a skill if it will repeat, confirm the new facts into the context files, and update your preferences file with the feedback you gave along the way. I say it almost in those words: “we’re done, turn this into a skill, and file the corrections I made.” That one sentence at the end of a task is the difference between a tool you use and a system that learns.

blocks.html_en: The organizing question surprised me. It isn’t “what topic does this belong to?” It’s “how fast does this change?” Everything in your work has a speed: your product’s positioning barely moves, a status summary lasts about a week, a ticket queue changes by the hour. File things by their speed, and stale can never masquerade as fresh. File them by topic, and old truth sits next to current truth, looking identical.

blocks.html_en: The three folders in the workspace are the three speeds. The concrete habit: the next meeting note you take goes into operations/ with the date in the filename, and the paragraph you keep retyping about your product goes into context/product.md. A note was true the day you wrote it, so the date travels in the filename where Claude reads it; the positioning paragraph is true until you change it, so it lives where every session can load it. Projects sit between the two speeds, which is why each project folder splits tasks.md from brief.md.

blocks.html_en: MCPs, those live connections from Step 4, sit at the fast end of the spectrum: they’re for what changes hourly. Files are for what changes slowly. If you’re pasting live data into a context file, an MCP should own it; if you’re re-fetching stable truth through an MCP every session, a file should own it. If you’ve used PARA, Tiago Forte’s filing method, this rhymes with it, with one difference: PARA sorts by actionability, because a human’s failure mode is losing track of what to act on. This system sorts by rate of change, because an LLM’s failure mode is stale context confidently reused.

blocks.html_en: CLAUDE.md is the one file every session loads: the map that says who you are, what lives where, and the few rules that always apply. Here’s the honest practice: you almost never touch it by hand. If you’re organizing an existing folder rather than using the starter workspace, the /init command creates it for you: Claude scans the folder and writes the map itself. From then on, maintenance happens as a side effect: when you add a skill or a context file, Claude updates the map to match, and your job is just to say yes.

blocks.html_en: The one thing worth knowing is why the map stays small. It loads into every session, relevant or not, so every line spends a little of what Anthropic’s context-engineering post calls the “attention budget”; their docs target under 200 lines and warn that bloated files make Claude ignore your actual instructions. The map points, the files carry: knowledge lives in context/, loaded only when a task needs it. I wrote about this just-in-time principle in How to build an AI helper for your team with Cowork; here, Claude applies it for you.

blocks.html_en: I carried a doubt about this practice for months. My habit is to look at every recurring piece of work and ask whether it can become a skill, so I give the feedback once and never redo the work again. It felt productive, and I wasn’t sure it was right, because nothing written for product people says where skills end and files begin. The test that settled it: nouns go in files, verbs go in skills. What Claude needs to know is a noun: product facts, user segments, terminology, in context/. What Claude needs to do is a verb: draft, review, synthesize, each one a skill.

blocks.html_en: In practice, skills come from the closing move of the first practice: you finish a task, you’re satisfied, and you ask Claude to turn what you just did together into a skill. The workspace’s status-update skill shows what one looks like: where it reads from, what shape the output takes, what quality bar it checks. Steps, a quality bar, an output format: that’s what a skill encodes, and that’s why “the roadmap review prep” or “the churn digest” qualify while “that one weird escalation” doesn’t. If you want to build one from scratch instead, How to build your first Claude Code skill walks through it step by step.

blocks.html_en: The first mismatch is a “skill” that’s really a fact bucket: product context wearing a skill’s clothes, never doing anything. That becomes a context file. The second is the reverse: a procedure written as notes inside context/, like a “how I run reviews” paragraph nobody can execute. A documented-but-not-executable procedure gets re-explained anyway, which defeats the whole point. That one becomes a skill. The know/do split is how documentation practice has organized itself for a decade (Diátaxis formalizes it); skills just make the “do” side executable.

blocks.html_en: The simplest version is the one to start with, and it’s the highest-return edit in this article. That’s one correction, filed once, applied to everything that follows. The oldest entries in my own preferences file are corrections I have never had to give again.

content_html_zh:
我的产品工作的 Claude Code 工作区是一个文件夹，里面几乎没有代码。 它包含一个上下文文件夹，其中包含有关公司的所有信息：产品、用户、竞争对手、我喜欢的工作方式。 每个项目一个文件夹，任务与可交付成果分开。 一组技能，每个技能执行一项重复工作：状态更新、PRD 审查、访谈综合。 当我提供一次反馈时，它会出现在一个文件中，并附有说明原因的注释，并且我再也不会提供该反馈。 我没有设计这个系统。 我之所以能做到这一点，主要是因为我先犯了错误。

犯错给了我一个教训，贯穿整篇文章。 除了基础知识之外，您在 Claude Code 中的结果将取决于您提示的程度而停止，并开始取决于您归档的程度。 一个好的提示可以改善一次会话；一个好的文件可以改善之后的每一次会话。 您已经阅读过的即时调整建议在归档开始变得重要的时候就不再有帮助了。

因此，我没有描述我的系统，而是将其打包。 初学者工作区在 GitHub 上公开：文件夹、上下文模板和五项 PM 技能，通过一次设置面试进行个性化。 您无需精通技术即可跟进；每个步骤都详细说明，包括安装工具。 虽然我的示例是产品工作，但相同的架构适合任何上下文繁重的工作：设计主管的研究库、数据团队的指标定义、创始人的所有文件夹。

这是路线。

  • 开关。 我将向您展示聊天模式和 Cowork 不能给您的功能，以及为什么终端对于产品经理来说是值得的。
  • 入门工作区。 下载它，运行一个设置技能，并给它一个真正的任务：六个步骤，每个步骤都显示在屏幕上。
  • 做法。 使系统复合的六个步骤，每个步骤都明确指出要做什么以及你会得到什么。
  • 节奏。 这是系统内部正常工作日的样子，从第一个简短的提示到两分钟的归档习惯。

回报是具体的。 一次就可以开始运行：安装工具、下载工作区、回答设置面试、移交第一个实际任务。 您不再在每次会议上重新解释您的公司，并且您所做的每一次更正都将成为永久性的。 每个步骤如下。

是时候打开文件柜了。

您今天可能通过 Claude 的聊天来运行您的产品工作：浏览器选项卡或桌面应用程序，也许是用于代理任务的 Cowork。 它有效，而这正是陷阱。 每一次对话都是从零开始。 您上次上传的策略文档消失了，您耐心解释的上下文存在于您再也找不到的线程中，您喜欢的输出被困在对话中而不是坐在文件中。 聊天是一个思考的好地方，也是一个积累的可怕地方。 对于偶尔的问题也没关系。 对于日常产品工作，这意味着每天早上都要支付相同的设置成本。

Claude Code 与 Claude 相同，但主目录不同：计算机上的一个文件夹，可以读取、导航和写入。 上下文存在于持久存在的文件中。 重复性工作依赖于按命令运行的技能。 输出作为您保存的文档而不是您滚动查找的消息出现。 在我的日常使用中，我以前在聊天或 Cowork 中所做的一切在这里运行得更好，因为没有任何事情会被解释两次。 这是我自己工作中的观察结果，不是法律，但它已经持续了几个月。

真正改变我工作的部分是下面的终端。 Claude Code 与 GitHub 原生交互，无需连接器：它可以提取公司存储库并回答有关它的问题，并且可以推送您自己的工作。 要求它获取产品背后的存储库并解释功能标志的实际用途。 将您的工作区推送到私有存储库，队友可以克隆它并继承您的领先优势。 对于产品经理来说，这是直接进入代码库的方式，也是共享整个系统的一种方式，而这两者都是聊天所不具备的。

没有人给你的是制造所有这些化合物的归档系统。 用 Anthropic 自己的话来说，其最佳实践指南是“为在各种代码库、语言和环境中使用 Claude Code 的工程师编写的”，并且工程师可以自由地使用他们的结构：代码库已经是有组织的上下文。 现有的 PM 指南（其中最著名的是 Sachin Rekhi）正确地告诉您“将所有产品数据和文档存储在本地 Markdown 文件中”，然后继续。 怎么组织的？ 在没有答案的情况下尝试一下，你就会得到我所拥有的：四十个松散的文件和一个陈旧的设置。 入门工作区就是这个答案，是预先构建的。 让我们来设置一下。

入门工作区是我运行自己的产品工作的结构，已清理为模板：文件夹、带有引导占位符的上下文文件、示例项目和已安装的五项技能。 整个事情是免费和公开的：claude-code-pm-starter。 六个步骤可带您从一无所有到第一个真正的任务，并且没有一个步骤需要技术背景。

开始之前请注意一个先决条件。 您需要 Claude Code 的付费 Claude 计划。 其他所有内容（包括您将安装的两个工具）都是免费的，并包含在步骤中。

Claude Code 在终端中运行，而对于产品经理来说，单独的终端是一个糟糕的家：你看不到你的文件。 修复方法是使用 IDE。 IDE 只是一个编辑器，在您工作时将文件夹显示为文件面板；开发人员一整天都住在其中，而您只是为了文件面板而借用它。 下载免费标准 VS Code，然后像安装任何应用程序一样安装它。 您不会在其中编写代码。 您将看到您的工作区在左侧面板中自行组织，这正是聊天模式从未给您提供的可见性。

打开存储库页面，单击绿色代码按钮，然后选择下载 ZIP。 无需 git，无需帐户。 解压缩并将文件夹移动到您保存工作的位置。 该文件夹即将成为您的产品工作所在的位置，因此请选择您会再次找到它的位置，例如主目录中的工作文件夹。

打开 VS Code，选择“文件”>“打开文件夹”，然后选择解压后的文件夹。 左侧面板现在显示整个结构：上下文/、项目/、操作/、技能。 然后使用 Terminal > New Terminal 打开 VS Code 中的终端，这里有一个改变整个感觉的小技巧：右键单击终端面板的标题并选择“向右移动面板”。 左边是文件，右边是代理：它不再感觉像命令行，而开始感觉像坐在文档旁边的同事。

如果您还没有 Claude Code，请立即按照官方指南进行安装；这是粘贴到该终端的一个命令。 然后输入 claude 并按 Enter。 Claude Code 从文件夹内部开始，读取映射文件，并从您的第一条消息中知道所有内容的位置。

一项区别可以让初学者避免很多困惑。 终端需要准确的命令；克劳德想要正常的语言。 在输入 claude 之前，您正在与终端对话，其中拼写和语法很重要。 现在 Claude Code 正在运行，您正在与 Claude 交谈，就像在聊天应用程序中一样。 因此，做自然的第一件事：输入 hello 并询问它可以在此文件夹中看到什么。 它会像刚刚阅读您的文件的同事一样回答。

一些斜杠命令值得第一天了解，直接输入 Claude Code：

  • /model - 显示您正在运行的 Claude 模型并允许您切换。
  • /effort - 设置克劳德在每个答案中投入多少思考；努力工作的努力程度越高，快速草稿的努力程度越低。
  • /mcp - 列出您的 MCP、Jira、Slack 或 Confluence 等工具的实时连接，并让您管理它们。
  • /plugins - 打开插件系统，这个值得一分钟。 Claude Code 默认附带 Anthropic 的插件目录，并且可以在顶部添加市场。 其中一个专为产品经理打造：pm-skills，涵盖发现、策略、执行和发布的一百多种 PM 技能；其自述文件包含最新的安装说明。 pm-execution 涵盖 PRD、OKR、路线图和回顾； pm-product-discovery 增加了访谈和假设测试。 安装与您的工作相匹配的两到三个，而不是全部九个；每个安装的插件都是系统携带的上下文。

再进行一次控制，您就完成了游览：按 Shift+Tab 循环 Claude Code 的三种模式。

  • 默认模式在触摸任何文件之前都会征求您的许可。
  • 自动接受无需询问即可应用编辑。
  • 计划模式是值得记住的模式：克劳德研究并提出一项计划，在您批准之前不会发生任何变化。

从默认开始，对任何大的事情使用计划模式，并为您已经学会信任的工作保存自动接受。 对于除此之外的所有内容，此社区备忘单是我发现的最好的一页参考资料。

输入 /setup-workspace 并按 Enter。 工作区附带一项技能，其唯一的工作就是个性化模板：它会采访您有关您的公司、您的产品、您的用户以及您喜欢的工作方式，然后填写上下文文件并将示例项目重命名为您最活跃的真实项目。 用通俗易懂的语言回答；它会进行写入并显示每个文件以进行“是”或“修复”。

您不必凭记忆回答：粘贴链接。 将您产品的公共站点、文档页面，或者，如果您在上一步中连接了 Atlassian MCP，则将其交给有关您团队的 Confluence 页面，它会读取它们并根据已编写的内容构建上下文文件。 十五分钟的时间完全解决了空白页问题。 您的具体问题与我的略有不同；每个会话都有点不可预测，这就是这些模型的工作原理。 跳过你还不知道的任何内容；诚实的占位符胜过发明的内容。

不要在设置时结束第一个会话；递给你实际上欠某人的东西。 输入 /status-update 并观察它从项目的任务文件而不是你的记忆中起草更新。 或者将其指向真正的可交付成果：

起草[您的项目]的启动简报。 在 context/preferences.md 中匹配我的写作偏好。 在得出任何结论之前，请检查项目的tasks.md 中的未解决问题。

第一个听起来像您的输出，关于您的产品，其中包含您的项目的真实状态，就是提交文件的那一刻。 文件夹中还有另外三项技能：prd-审阅您想要仔细阅读的下一份文档、采访-综合您的下一次用户对话，以及文件反馈，使您的更正永久有效。

这就是开始：一次性建立一个工作系统。 让它复合的关键在于你如何喂养它，这就是六种做法。

入门结构通过首先将每一个都弄错来对我所集中的实践进行编码。 它们不是一种必须遵守的方法论，而是一种必须遵守的方法论。它们是不断赢得一席之地的举措。 下面的每一项都列出了要做的具体事情以及你会得到什么。 第一个是发动机；其余的人掌舵。

回报最高的习惯也是最简单的表述：默认在工作空间中处理所有事情。 每次有任务降临到您身上时，您都可以打开工作区并使用 Claude Code 在那里完成任务，即使聊天会感觉更快。 一种新任务的第一次运行需要更长的时间，我不会假装：你解释，你纠正，你调整。 但每个解释都会保存在一个文件中，因此第二次运行会提前开始，而第三次运行几乎不需要你。 这就像教实习生：第一个代表团花了你一个下午的时间，然后工作就完成了。 保持聊天模式的任务不会告诉系统任何东西；在工作空间中完成相同的任务是一项投资，每次重复都会带来回报。

这个习惯有一个结束动作，这是复利实际发生的地方。 当任务完成并且您对结果感到满意时，不要只是关闭终端。 让克劳德将学到的知识储存起来：将已完成的任务转化为技能（如果它会重复），将新事实确认到上下文文件中，并使用您在此过程中提供的反馈更新您的首选项文件。 我几乎用这句话来表达：“我们完成了，把它变成一项技能，并将我所做的更正归档。” 任务结束时的一句话就是你使用的工具和学习系统之间的区别。

这个组织问题让我感到惊讶。 这不是“这属于什么主题？” 问题是“这种变化有多快？” 你工作中的一切都有一个速度：你的产品的定位几乎没有变化，状态摘要持续大约一周，工单队列每小时都在变化。 按速度归档，陈旧的东西永远无法伪装成新鲜的东西。 按主题将它们归档，旧的事实与当前的事实相邻，看起来相同。

工作区中的三个文件夹是三种速度。 具体习惯是：您记录的下一次会议记录将进入操作/，文件名中包含日期，而您不断重新输入的有关产品的段落将进入 context/product.md。 注释在您写下的那天是正确的，因此日期会出现在 Claude 读取它的文件名中；定位段落在您更改之前都是正确的，因此它位于每个会话都可以加载它的位置。 项目位于两种速度之间，这就是每个项目文件夹将tasks.md 与brief.md 分开的原因。

还有第三种速度，您已经拥有了。

MCP，即第 4 步中的实时连接，位于该范围的快速端：它们针对的是每小时发生变化的情况。 文件是为了那些缓慢变化的东西。 如果您将实时数据粘贴到上下文文件中，则 MCP 应该拥有它；如果您每次会话都通过 MCP 重新获取稳定的事实，则文件应该拥有它。 如果你使用过蒂亚戈·福尔特 (Tiago Forte) 的归档方法 PARA，你会发现这与它押韵，但有一点不同：PARA 按可操作性排序，因为人类的失败模式是不知道该采取什么行动。 该系统按变化率排序，因为法学硕士的失败模式是陈旧的上下文可以自信地重用。

CLAUDE.md 是每个会话都会加载的一个文件：一张地图，说明您是谁、什么生活在哪里以及始终适用的几条规则。 这是诚实的做法：你几乎从不用手触摸它。 如果您正在组织现有文件夹而不是使用起始工作区，则 /init 命令会为您创建它：Claude 扫描文件夹并自行写入地图。 从那时起，维护就会作为副作用发生：当您添加技能或上下文文件时，克劳德会更新地图以匹配，而您的工作就是说“是”。

值得了解的一件事是为什么地图很小。 它会加载到每个会话中，无论相关与否，因此每一行都会花费一点 Anthropic 的上下文工程帖子所称的“注意力预算”；他们的文档目标是 200 行以下，并警告臃肿的文件会使 Claude 忽略您的实际指令。 地图点、文件携带：知识存在于上下文/中，仅在任务需要时加载。 我在《How to build an AI helper for your team with Cowork》中写到了这一及时原则；在这里，克劳德为你应用它。

几个月来我一直对这种做法抱有疑问。 我的习惯是看每一件重复的工作，问它是否能成为一种技能，所以我反馈一次就不再重做。 它感觉很有成效，但我不确定它是否正确，因为没有为产品人员编写的内容说明技能在哪里结束，文件在哪里开始。 解决这个问题的测试：名词放在文件中，动词放在技能中。 克劳德需要知道的是一个名词：产品事实、用户细分、术语、上下文/。 克劳德要做的就是一个动词：起草、审阅、综合，每一项都是一项技能。

在实践中，技能来自于第一次练习的结束动作：你完成了一项任务，你感到满意，然后你要求克劳德将你们刚刚一起做的事情变成一项技能。 工作区的状态更新技能显示了它的样子：它从哪里读取，输出采用什么形状，它检查什么质量栏。 步骤、质量栏、输出格式：这就是技能编码的内容，这就是为什么“路线图审查准备”或“流失摘要”符合资格，而“那个奇怪的升级”则不符合资格。 如果您想从头开始构建一个，如何构建您的第一个克劳德代码技能将逐步介绍它。

该测试还发现了东西最终被放入错误抽屉的两种方式。

第一个不匹配是“技能”，这实际上是一个事实桶：产品环境穿着技能的衣服，从不做任何事情。 这成为一个上下文文件。 第二个是相反的：在 context/ 中以注释形式编写的程序，就像“我如何运行评论”段落，没有人可以执行。 无论如何，一个已记录但不可执行的程序都会被重新解释，这违背了整个要点。 那成为一种技能。 知识/行动的分离是文档实践十年来组织自身的方式（Diátaxis 将其形式化）；技能只是让“做”的部分变得可执行。

你知道那一刻。 克劳德起草了你的状态更新，你修改了你已经修改过一次的相同措辞。 这是每周都会改变我的重构：在聊天中进行的更正是容易消失的；当会话结束时它就消失了。 系统的整个复利回报来自于使纠正永久化，这就是实践停止组织并开始学习的地方。

最简单的版本是一开始的版本，也是本文中回报率最高的编辑版本。 打开 context/preferences.md 并写下三行内容：句子长度、打开文档的内容、禁止使用的单词。 从那时起，克劳德起草的每一份文件都符合您的写作偏好，而不是听起来像新闻稿。 这是一次更正，提交一次，适用于随后的所有内容。 我自己的首选项文件中最旧的条目是我不必再次给出的更正。

对于第一次编辑之后的所有内容，工作区都会提供一项为您归档的技能。 当您发现自己正在纠正某些内容时，请运行 /file-feedback。 它通过四个问题进行更正。

这是一次性的单据吗？ 放手吧;并非所有事情都值得归档。 一个缺失的事实？ 它会转到匹配的上下文文件或项目简介。 一个错误的过程？ 该修复已纳入技能中，因此每次都能正确运行。 品尝？ 它成为一个偏好条目，这里是重要的细节：每个条目都有一行关于原因和一行关于如何应用它，因此未来的会话可以判断边缘情况而不是盲目地进行模式匹配。

事实证明，供应商也同意这一点，而且措辞几乎相同。 Anthropic 的记忆文档会告诉你，当“克劳德第二次犯同样的错误”或“你在聊天中输入与上次会话相同的更正或说明”时，把事情写下来。 最佳实践指南仅用一句话就承诺了回报：“文件的价值会随着时间的推移而增值。” 这是我贴在便利贴上的版本，以及我将交给你的团队的那句话：如果你已经说了两次，它就属于一个文件。

最后一个练习消除了你头脑中的障碍，而不是你文件中的障碍。 你会发现自己认为某件事是遥不可及的：太技术性、太长、需要教程、需要工程师。 此举是先询问克劳德·科德，让答案让你感到惊讶。 我想尝试 AWS Amplify，这是 Amazon 的用于构建和托管应用程序的服务，但我的反应还是老样子：遵循指南、阅读文档、预算时间，而我却没有。 相反，我将文档链接粘贴到 Claude Code 中，并要求提供两件事：一个用于测试服务的工作原型，以及为非技术人员编写的分步指南。 一次，我就得到了一些我可以真正发布的东西，以及一份我可以遵循和理解的指南。 我预算的时间从来没有花过。

同样的反应适用于各种规模，而不仅仅是新工具。 在你自己总结四十页的研究报告之前，先问问。 在你认为数据问题需要分析师之前，先问问。 在检查每个中间步骤之前，给整个任务设置约束并验证结果。 你通过前五次实践构建的系统正是让询问变得便宜的原因：上下文已归档，偏好已知，错误的答案会让你需要更正，然后系统会保留该更正。 六种实践，一种架构。 这就是正常工作日的感觉。

在系统中的一天看起来不太像聊天，而更像是与一位速度很快的同事一起工作，他首先读取文件。

会话在项目文件夹中开始，而不是空白聊天。 我在 VS Code 中打开工作区，在终端中启动 claude，然后地图会加载每个可供使用的文件路径。 任务文件已经说明了情况、被阻止的内容以及接下来会发生什么，因为上一个会话已更新它。 我的第一个提示命名了目标并按名称指向文件，并且故意保持简短。 随着申请量的增加，提示也会减少。 在这个系统中，一个好的提示包括三个部分：一句话的目标、不可协商的约束以及在向您展示之前要验证的内容。 大约一百字，通常更少。 步骤在于技能，背景在于文件，提示只需引导。 对于更大的工作，我添加了一项操作：使用 Shift+Tab 切换到计划模式，并在运行任何内容之前批准计划。

将所有这些整合在一起的习惯在会话结束时需要两分钟，而文件反馈技能占据了大部分时间。 三个问题：我是否纠正了之前纠正过的任何内容，是否出现了未在任何地方归档的新事实，是否再次重复了某项工作？ 通过刳刨机重复修正；重复的工作被提名为下一个技能。 当答案是三个“否”时（这是大多数会议），请跳过仪式。

每隔十几次左右，我就会花十五分钟进行修剪，我认为这是最不可选的部分。 过时的上下文比丢失上下文更糟糕。 对克劳德来说，过期的竞争对手笔记或过时的定位线并不显得陈旧；它被充满信心地融入到新的工作中，而 Anthropic 的最佳实践指南也带有相应的警告：当两条规则相互矛盾时，克劳德可能会任意选择一条。 因此：对已过日期的内容添加日期标记，归档已关闭的项目，删除您不想在草稿中引用的任何内容。 这就是整个系统，正在运行。 剩下的就是开始它。

对我来说改变的并不是克劳德变得更聪明了。 而是我两次不再进行同样的对话。 我用来重新输入的公司解释位于 context/ 中。 我用来重复的反馈存在于技能和首选项文件中。 这些项目从中断的地方继续。 该系统的实际产品是安静的：更短的提示，更少的更正，会话在工作中间开始，而不是在我的工作描述的开头。

这种形式远远超出了产品管理的范围。 注重发现的 PM 将访谈综合归档为过时的输出，并让技能进行综合。 平台 PM 的稳定上下文是 API 使用者和版本控制策略。 创始人将投资者的更新转变为由指标文件提供的技能。 设计主管只对标准提出一次批评，而不是在每次审查中重新解释它们。 数据主管的指标定义成为每个团队成员的会话读取的上下文文件。 不同的工作，相同的三个抽屉，相同的习惯。

从小事做起，让自己感觉雄心勃勃。 下载入门工作区，运行设置访谈，然后添加关于您如何写作的三行内容。 然后将它带入你的下一个任务，以及之后的任务。 下次当你发现自己第二次告诉克劳德·科德某件事时，你就会确切地知道它的去向。 很快，你就会不记得上次说这句话是什么时候了。

没有帖子
